I-1.explain: A comatose child loses airway tone and protective reflexes, so the airway kills first; neurology can wait until ABC is secured.
I-1.hook: A before brain: airway first, always.

checks.q: In an unconscious child, which problem is addressed before neurology?
checks.why: Loss of tone and reflexes obstructs the airway; airway comes before any neurological work-up.

I-1.explain: Coma causes split into metabolic/toxic and structural; AEIOU-TIPS lists them so none is forgotten at the bedside.

checks.q: Which mnemonic lists the causes of coma?
checks.why: AEIOU-TIPS is the coma list; MUDPILES is for raised anion gap acidosis.

checks.q: In AEIOU-TIPS, what does the 'I' stand for?
checks.why: I = insulin (hypo/hyperglycaemia); infection is the I of TIPS.

I-1.explain: Focal lesions damage one side; toxins and metabolic upsets hit the whole brain. Rising ICP squeezes perfusion and pushes brain through openings.
I-1.hook: Cushing triad: high BP, slow pulse, odd breathing.

checks.q: Global, symmetric signs in coma suggest which cause type?
checks.why: Metabolic/toxic causes act diffusely; structural lesions give focal, asymmetric signs.

checks.q: Which triad signals raised ICP?
checks.why: Cushing triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration as CPP = MAP - ICP falls.

checks.q: Uncal herniation compresses which cranial nerve, dilating the pupil?
checks.why: Uncus compresses the oculomotor nerve (CN III) → dilated pupil; tonsillar herniation → arrest.

I-1.explain: Specific signs point to the cause: drug toxidromes, posturing level, and skin clues of sepsis or abuse.

checks.q: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression suggest which poisoning?
checks.why: Opioids cause miosis plus CNS/respiratory depression; anticholinergics dilate pupils.

checks.q: Which posture shows flexed arms?
checks.why: Decorticate = flexed arms; decerebrate = extended arms (lower, worse lesion).

checks.q: On exposure, odd bruises in a comatose child should raise concern for?
checks.why: Expose fully: odd bruises suggest abuse, purpura suggests meningococcus.

I-1.explain: Hypoglycaemia is quick to find and fix; CT finds structural causes; LP can cause herniation if pressure is high.

checks.q: Which bedside test must never be skipped in coma?
checks.why: Hypoglycaemia is common, reversible and brain-damaging, so bedside glucose is mandatory.

checks.q: Head CT is indicated at which GCS threshold?
checks.why: Per notes, CT if GCS ≤ 14, skull fracture or focal signs; ≤ 8 is the intubation threshold.

checks.q: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with raised ICP or what?
checks.why: Never LP with raised ICP (herniation risk) or shock; fever is the reason to consider LP.

I-1.explain: Protect airway, reverse what's reversible, treat infection early and lower ICP by head elevation, CO₂ reduction and osmotherapy.

checks.q: At what GCS should an unconscious child be intubated?
checks.why: GCS ≤ 8 means airway reflexes are unreliable → intubation.

checks.q: If meningitis is possible, when is ceftriaxone given?
checks.why: Don't delay antibiotics for LP; give ceftriaxone immediately.

checks.q: Which osmotic drug is used to lower raised ICP?
checks.why: Raised ICP: head up, mannitol (osmotic); hyperventilation only briefly for impending herniation.

I-2.explain: Seizures beyond 5 min rarely stop alone and get harder to stop, so treatment starts at 5 min and escalates every 5 min.

checks.q: Status epilepticus is defined as a seizure lasting at least how long?
checks.why: Operational definition: ≥ 5 min, when treatment should start; 30 min is the old definition.

I-2.explain: Age predicts cause: neonates have structural/metabolic insults, toddlers fever, older children epilepsy or lesions.
I-2.hook: Neonatal seizure = always look for a cause.

checks.q: A neonatal seizure is best described as?
checks.why: Neonatal seizures always have a cause: HIE, hypoglycaemia, low Ca/Na, sepsis, bleed.

checks.q: What is the commonest seizure type in toddlers?
checks.why: Febrile seizures affect 3-5% of children and dominate this age.

checks.q: Which is a cause of seizures in older children per the notes?
checks.why: Older children: epilepsy, trauma, tumour, AVM; HIE is neonatal.

I-2.explain: Young brains wire excitation before inhibition, so the threshold is low; fever or metabolic stress tips it over.

checks.q: Why is the seizure threshold low in infants?
checks.why: Excitatory synapses mature before inhibitory ones → low threshold.

checks.q: What tends to trigger febrile seizures?
checks.why: Notes/traditional teaching: a rapid rise crosses the threshold (evidence for rate over peak height is weak).

I-2.explain: Seizure types look distinct: absence is brief staring, focal has automatisms, West has spasms with chaotic EEG.
I-2.hook: Absence: blow on a windmill to provoke it.

checks.q: Absence seizures are provoked by what?
checks.why: Absence: blank stare, provoked by hyperventilation in clinic.

checks.q: Mouth chewing and staring suggest which seizure type?
checks.why: Automatisms (chewing, head tilt) with confusion = focal impaired awareness.

checks.q: Which EEG pattern goes with West syndrome?
checks.why: West: spasms + hypsarrhythmia; 3 Hz spike-wave is absence.

I-2.explain: Correct reversible causes first (glucose, salts, infection), then image and EEG a first unexplained seizure.

checks.q: When is bedside glucose checked in a seizing child?
checks.why: Glucose at 0 min alongside Ca, Na and an infection screen.

checks.q: For a first seizure, which emergency imaging is used?
checks.why: Emergency: non-contrast CT head; MRI electively; plus EEG.

I-2.explain: Escalate by time: two benzodiazepine doses, then a second-line agent, then anaesthesia. Specific syndromes have specific drugs.
I-2.hook: ACTH for West; phenobarbital for neonates.

checks.q: At 15 min of status, which drug is given?
checks.why: 5 & 10 min: benzodiazepines; 15 min: levetiracetam/phenytoin/valproate; 25 min: RSI.

checks.q: First-line anticonvulsant in neonatal seizures?
checks.why: Neonates: phenobarbital, pyridoxine if resistant; ACTH is for West syndrome.

I-3.explain: Most childhood headaches are primary and benign; the job is to spot the rare secondary one.

checks.q: Migraine and tension-type headache are which category?
checks.why: Primary headaches (migraine, tension) are benign; secondary have an underlying cause.

I-3.explain: Benign primary headache dominates; tumours in children sit in the posterior fossa, giving hydrocephalus early.

checks.q: Which headache types form the overwhelming majority in children?
checks.why: Primary headaches, migraine and tension-type, are by far most common.

checks.q: Childhood CNS tumours are usually located where?
checks.why: Pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma, ependymoma: posterior fossa.

checks.q: Which secondary cause is listed alongside IIH?
checks.why: Also IIH and medication overuse headache.

I-3.explain: Lying flat and coughing raise ICP further; the long intracranial course of CN VI makes it stretch first.

checks.q: Raised ICP headache is typically worse when?
checks.why: Lying flat overnight raises ICP → worse on waking, with vomiting without nausea.

checks.q: Which cranial nerve palsy is a false localising sign of raised ICP?
checks.why: Abducens has a long course and stretches with raised ICP.

I-3.explain: Paediatric migraine is shorter and more often bilateral than adult migraine; tension is steady and featureless.
I-3.hook: Kids' migraine: shorter and both sides.

checks.q: In children, migraine can last as short as?
checks.why: Adults 4-72 h; children often bilateral and as short as 2 h.

checks.q: Chronic tension-type headache occurs on how many days per month?
checks.why: Chronic = ≥ 15 days/month for more than 3 months.

I-3.explain: A structured history (tempo, progression) plus red flags decides who needs imaging; MRI avoids radiation and sees posterior fossa better.

checks.q: Which is one of the three key headache history questions?
checks.why: Ask: acute or chronic, progressive or not, any red flags.

checks.q: Which age is a headache red flag?
checks.why: Red flags include awakening from sleep, ataxia, focal signs, age under 5.

checks.q: Preferred imaging when a headache red flag is present?
checks.why: Urgent neuroimaging, preferably MRI.

I-3.explain: Simple analgesia first, triptans if needed; IIH is treated by cutting CSF production; diaries guide triggers and prophylaxis.

checks.q: First-line for acute migraine in children?
checks.why: NSAIDs or acetaminophen first-line; triptans also possible.

checks.q: Drug of choice for idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
checks.why: Acetazolamide reduces CSF production (± furosemide).

checks.q: What tool identifies headache triggers?
checks.why: A diary reveals triggers and frequency; prophylaxis if frequent.

I-4.explain: Young infants cannot localise infection and look deceptively well, so fever alone drives the work-up.

checks.q: Below what age can infants not localise infection?
checks.why: Under 3 months, infants can't localise; fever threshold ≥ 38 °C.

I-4.explain: Neonatal pathogens come from the birth canal; UTI is the most common serious bacterial infection overall.
I-4.hook: GBS, E. coli, Listeria: the birth canal trio.

checks.q: Which organism is a classic cause of neonatal sepsis?
checks.why: Neonatal sepsis: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; consider HSV.

checks.q: Commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infants?
checks.why: Urinary tract infection is the commonest SBI.

I-4.explain: Immature immunity, no vaccines yet and no localising signs mean looking well does not exclude serious infection.

checks.q: In young febrile infants, clinical appearance is?
checks.why: Immature immunity and no localising signs make appearance unreliable.

I-4.explain: Infant meningitis is vague; specific red flags like a non-blanching rash or prolonged fever point to dangerous diagnoses.

checks.q: Which sign is usually absent in infant meningitis?
checks.why: Infants present with poor feeding, 'not right'; no neck stiffness.

checks.q: Fever over 5 days in an infant suggests?
checks.why: Prolonged fever >5 days → think Kawasaki; non-blanching rash → meningococcus.

I-4.explain: Work-up intensity falls with age: neonates get everything including LP; older infants are risk-stratified.
I-4.hook: Under 28 days: everyone gets the LP.

checks.q: Which febrile infants all get a lumbar puncture?
checks.why: Under 28 days: full septic screen incl. LP for all (AAP 2021: selective at 22-28 days).

checks.q: In febrile infants aged 1-3 months, when is LP done?
checks.why: 1-3 months: FBC, CRP, culture, urine; LP if unwell.

checks.q: How should urine be collected in a febrile child over 3 months?
checks.why: Clean catch, not a bag (contamination).

I-4.explain: Neonatal antibiotics must cover Listeria, which cephalosporins miss, hence ampicillin; well older infants with a viral source can go home.

checks.q: Which antibiotic is added for febrile neonates to cover Listeria?
checks.why: IV ampicillin + gentamicin/cefotaxime; ± aciclovir.

checks.q: Listeria is resistant to which antibiotic class?
checks.why: Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins, so ampicillin is needed.

checks.q: Management of a well infant over 3 months with viral source?
checks.why: Well, >3 months, viral source → home with safety-netting.

I-5.explain: Blanching tells you if blood has leaked from vessels (petechiae/purpura) — that changes urgency more than any other feature.

checks.q: What is the first question with fever and rash?
checks.why: Non-blanching = possible meningococcus; ask first, pattern-match after.

I-5.explain: The numbered diseases are historical exanthems; chickenpox is VZV spread by air; a few rashes are emergencies.

checks.q: Which is the 'fifth disease'?
checks.why: Fifth = parvovirus B19; sixth = roseola (exanthema subitum).

checks.q: How is chickenpox transmitted?
checks.why: VZV is airborne (and by contact with vesicle fluid).

checks.q: Which rash with fever is an emergency?
checks.why: Emergencies: meningococcaemia, Kawasaki, SJS/TEN, toxic shock.

I-5.explain: Purpura means vessel leak; in sepsis that is lethal, but straining can do it in SVC territory (above the nipple line). Chickenpox comes in waves.

checks.q: Non-blanching rash with fever is what until proven otherwise?
checks.why: Fever + non-blanching rash = meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise.

checks.q: Petechiae above the nipple line after coughing are due to?
checks.why: Straining raises SVC-territory venous pressure → benign petechiae.

checks.q: Chickenpox lesions are typically in what pattern?
checks.why: Crops in different stages; smallpox lesions are all the same stage.

I-5.explain: Each exanthem has a signature: where it starts, mucosal clues, nodes or face pattern.

checks.q: Where does the measles rash start?
checks.why: Measles starts behind the ears/hairline; Koplik spots; death from pneumonia.

checks.q: Strawberry tongue and sandpaper rash suggest?
checks.why: Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue; parvo: slapped cheek.

checks.q: Rubella characteristically causes which lymphadenopathy?
checks.why: Rubella: suboccipital/postauricular nodes; Coxsackie A: hand, foot and mouth.

I-5.explain: After the glass test, morphology, start site and rash-fever timing narrow it; incubation helps with contacts.

checks.q: What simple test checks if a rash blanches?
checks.why: Press a glass: rash visible through it = non-blanching.

checks.q: Incubation period of measles?
checks.why: Measles 10-14 d; scarlet 2-5 d; rubella 14-21 d; varicella 10-21 d.

I-5.explain: Meningococcal sepsis needs antibiotics before anything else; chickenpox and Kawasaki have specific time-critical treatments.

checks.q: Immediate treatment for suspected meningococcal sepsis?
checks.why: Give benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone immediately.

checks.q: What does a newborn of a mother with chickenpox receive?
checks.why: Newborn of infected mother: VZIG; severe chickenpox: IV aciclovir.

checks.q: Kawasaki: IVIG should be given within how many days?
checks.why: IVIG within 10 days of fever onset to prevent coronary aneurysm.

I-6.explain: FUO needs both duration and a negative initial work-up; Kawasaki is a clinical diagnosis by criteria count.

checks.q: FUO requires fever >38 °C for at least how long?
checks.why: FUO: fever >38 °C ≥ 8 days with no cause after initial evaluation.

checks.q: Kawasaki: fever ≥ 5 days plus how many principal features?
checks.why: Classic Kawasaki needs fever ≥ 5 days plus 4 of 5 features.

I-6.explain: Common things first: infection outnumbers inflammatory disease and cancer in FUO.

checks.q: What is the commonest cause of FUO?
checks.why: Infection ~50%, inflammatory ~20%, malignancy ~10%.

checks.q: Kawasaki classically affects which children?
checks.why: Kawasaki is most common in children of East Asian descent.

I-6.explain: Kawasaki is a medium-vessel vasculitis with coronary predilection. In sJIA, a falling ESR with rising ferritin signals MAS (consumption).
I-6.hook: Falling ESR in sJIA = danger, not recovery.

checks.q: Which vessels does Kawasaki damage most?
checks.why: Coronary aneurysm → rupture or MI.

checks.q: sJIA with falling ESR and high ferritin suggests?
checks.why: Falling ESR (fibrinogen consumed), cytopenias, high ferritin → MAS.

I-6.explain: Kawasaki eyes are dry and spare the limbus; platelets rise late; sJIA has a daily fever spike with an evanescent rash.
I-6.hook: Kawasaki eyes: red but no pus.

checks.q: Kawasaki conjunctivitis is typically?
checks.why: Bilateral, non-purulent, limbal sparing.

checks.q: When does thrombocytosis appear in Kawasaki?
checks.why: Platelets rise in the second week; CRP/ESR high, sterile pyuria.

checks.q: sJIA rash is described as?
checks.why: Daily spiking fevers with a salmon-pink evanescent rash.

I-6.explain: In FUO, repeated bedside reassessment catches evolving clues better than blind tests; Kawasaki needs serial echo to catch aneurysms.

checks.q: Highest-yield investigation in FUO?
checks.why: Daily repeated history and exam picks up evolving clues.

checks.q: Kawasaki echo timing after diagnosis?
checks.why: Echo at diagnosis, then 1-2 and 4-6 weeks.

I-6.explain: IVIG damps the vasculitis and prevents aneurysms; aspirin is the one paediatric use despite Reye risk. Infants are atypical and highest risk.

checks.q: IVIG dose in Kawasaki?
checks.why: IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within 10 days.

checks.q: Kawasaki not defervescing after IVIG: next step?
checks.why: No defervescence → second IVIG; refractory → steroids/infliximab.

checks.q: Live vaccines after IVIG are delayed for how long?
checks.why: Notes: delay ~8 months as IVIG antibodies block the response (CDC: 11 months after 2 g/kg).

I-7.explain: Respiratory distress shows as fast breathing plus work-of-breathing signs; >60/min is tachypnoea in a newborn.
I-7.hook: Over 60 = too fast for a newborn.

checks.q: Neonatal tachypnoea threshold?
checks.why: Newborn tachypnoea is >60 breaths/min.

I-7.explain: Gestation and delivery mode predict the cause: preterm → RDS, term section → TTN, post-term → meconium.

checks.q: Meconium aspiration typically affects which babies?
checks.why: MAS: term and post-term; RDS: prematurity.

checks.q: Which is a structural cause of neonatal distress?
checks.why: Structural: CDH, choanal atresia, TE fistula; also sepsis and cyanotic CHD.

I-7.explain: No surfactant → alveoli collapse; retained fluid → TTN; failure of pulmonary pressure to fall → PPHN.

checks.q: What is lacking in RDS?
checks.why: Prematurity → inadequate surfactant → alveolar collapse.

checks.q: TTN is caused by?
options: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid
checks.why: TTN: delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.

checks.q: In PPHN, what fails to fall after birth?
checks.why: PVR stays high → right-to-left shunt; meconium also inactivates surfactant.

I-7.explain: Signs point to anatomy: empty abdomen in CDH, crying relieves choanal atresia, feeding-linked choking in TEF.

checks.q: TTN settles within how long?
checks.why: TTN: term section baby, grunting, settles in 24-72 h.

checks.q: Scaphoid abdomen in a distressed newborn suggests?
checks.why: Bowel in the chest → scaphoid abdomen = CDH.

checks.q: Coughing, choking and cyanosis with feeds suggest?
checks.why: TE fistula: coughing, choking, cyanosis.

I-7.explain: CXR, hyperoxia and NG tube position quickly separate lung, heart and oesophagus causes.

checks.q: RDS chest X-ray shows?
checks.why: RDS: ground-glass with air bronchograms; L:S ratio ≥ 2 means maturity.

checks.q: No response to 100% oxygen suggests?
checks.why: Failure to improve on 100% O₂ → cardiac (duct-dependent); PPHN → echo.

checks.q: NG tube coiling in the oesophagus indicates?
checks.why: A coiled NG tube = blind-ending oesophagus.

I-7.explain: Support breathing, give surfactant/steroids for RDS, avoid inflating bowel in CDH, treat sepsis and dilate pulmonary vessels in PPHN.

checks.q: Surfactant is given in RDS when FiO₂ exceeds?
checks.why: CPAP for all; surfactant when FiO₂ > 0.30; antenatal steroids to mother.

checks.q: Which is contraindicated in CDH resuscitation?
checks.why: Bag-mask inflates bowel in the chest; intubate with NG on suction.

checks.q: Specific treatment for PPHN?
checks.why: Inhaled NO dilates pulmonary vessels; sepsis gets ampicillin + gentamicin.

I-8.explain: Timing and bilirubin type point to cause; UGT is the liver enzyme turning unconjugated into conjugated bilirubin.

checks.q: Which enzyme conjugates bilirubin?
checks.why: UDP-glucuronyltransferase conjugates bilirubin; β-glucuronidase undoes it.

I-8.explain: Day-1 jaundice is haemolysis or sepsis; unconjugated types are production/conjugation issues; conjugated means liver or bile flow.

checks.q: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is?
checks.why: Day-1 jaundice: Rh/ABO, G6PD, spherocytosis, sepsis.

checks.q: Breast milk jaundice is linked to which enzyme?
checks.why: Breast milk β-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin → reabsorption.

checks.q: Which causes conjugated jaundice?
checks.why: Conjugated: biliary atresia, hepatitis, choledochal cyst, TORCH, galactosaemia.

I-8.explain: Light converts bilirubin into water-soluble isomers; free unconjugated bilirubin crosses into basal ganglia; Rh sensitisation needs a prior exposure.
I-8.hook: Rh: first baby sensitises, second suffers.

checks.q: How does phototherapy work?
checks.why: Light isomerises bilirubin to water-soluble forms excreted without conjugation.

checks.q: High unconjugated bilirubin causes?
checks.why: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble → crosses BBB → kernicterus.

checks.q: Rh disease affects which pregnancy?
checks.why: Rh- mother sensitised in a prior pregnancy; Rh+ fetus affected later.

I-8.explain: Pale stools mean no bile reaching the gut; cephalohaematoma is bounded by sutures; bilirubin encephalopathy gives abnormal tone and cry.
I-8.hook: Pale stools + dark urine = blocked bile.

checks.q: Prolonged jaundice, pale stools and dark urine suggest?
checks.why: Beyond 2 weeks with pale stools/dark urine = biliary atresia.

checks.q: Which swelling does not cross suture lines?
checks.why: Cephalohaematoma is subperiosteal, so bounded by sutures.

I-8.explain: Early jaundice needs a haemolysis screen; every prolonged case needs a split bilirubin to catch conjugated causes.

checks.q: Which test is part of the early jaundice work-up?
checks.why: Blood group, direct Coombs, FBC, film.

checks.q: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is >20% of total or above?
checks.why: Conjugated: >25 μmol/L or >20% of total.

I-8.explain: Treat by threshold charts, escalate to exchange; feed more; prevent Rh sensitisation; fix biliary atresia early.

checks.q: When is exchange transfusion indicated?
checks.why: Phototherapy above the line; exchange if it fails or encephalopathy.

checks.q: Management of breast milk jaundice?
checks.why: Breast milk jaundice: continue; breastfeeding jaundice: increase feeds.

checks.q: Kasai portoenterostomy should be done before?
checks.why: Kasai before 60 days gives best results; anti-D at 28-32 weeks and within 72 h.

I-9.explain: Central cyanosis reflects low arterial saturation, seen in warm, well-perfused mucosa unlike peripheral blueness.
I-9.hook: Look at the tongue, not the toes.

checks.q: Central cyanosis indicates?
checks.why: Central (lips, mucosa) = low arterial saturation.

I-9.explain: Blue babies have lung, heart, pulmonary pressure or blood causes; the cardiac ones are the five Ts.

checks.q: Polycythaemia causing cyanosis is haematocrit above?
checks.why: Polycythaemia: haematocrit >65%.

checks.q: Commonest cyanotic heart disease overall?
checks.why: ToF is commonest overall; transposition presents on day 1.

I-9.explain: High pulmonary pressure shunts blood past the lungs; duct-dependent lesions collapse as the duct closes.

checks.q: PPHN causes right-to-left shunt through which routes?
checks.why: PVR stays high → R→L shunt at PDA and PFO.

checks.q: When does the ductus usually close, causing collapse?
checks.why: Duct closes day 2-3 → duct-dependent babies collapse.

I-9.explain: Breathing is driven mainly by CO₂, so cyanotic heart babies breathe quietly; methaemoglobin looks brown with a normal PaO₂.

checks.q: A 'comfortably blue' newborn suggests which cause?
checks.why: Respiratory drive responds mainly to CO₂, so cardiac cyanosis is comfortable.

checks.q: Chocolate-brown blood with normal PaO₂ suggests?
checks.why: Methaemoglobinaemia: brown blood, normal PaO₂.

I-9.explain: Oxygen fixes lung disease but not fixed shunts; pre/post-ductal difference reveals shunt at the duct; echo defines anatomy.

checks.q: Which cyanosis improves on 100% oxygen?
checks.why: Hyperoxia test: pulmonary improves; cardiac and PPHN do not.

checks.q: Pre-ductal saturation is measured on which limb?
checks.why: Right hand = pre-ductal; difference >10% suggests PPHN.

checks.q: Key investigation in neonatal cyanosis?
checks.why: Echo defines cardiac anatomy and PPHN.

I-9.explain: Keep the duct open with PGE1; open the atrial septum to mix blood in TGA; dilate lung vessels with NO; reduce methaemoglobin with methylene blue.

checks.q: Drug to keep the duct open?
checks.why: PGE1 keeps duct open; indometacin/ibuprofen close it.

checks.q: Transposition: what is done before arterial switch?
checks.why: Septostomy improves mixing before the arterial switch.

checks.q: Treatment of methaemoglobinaemia?
checks.why: Methylene blue reduces methaemoglobin; NO is for PPHN.

I-10.explain: Defining thresholds triggers treatment; HHS is extreme glucose and osmolality without much ketosis.

checks.q: Neonatal hypoglycaemia threshold?
checks.why: Neonatal hypoglycaemia: blood glucose below 2.6 mmol/L.

checks.q: HHS: glucose above which level?
checks.why: HHS: glucose >600 mg/dL, osmolarity >320.

I-10.explain: Ketones show whether fat is being burned: ketotic hypos are fasting problems; non-ketotic mean insulin excess or blocked fat oxidation.

checks.q: Commonest age for ketotic hypoglycaemia?
checks.why: Ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood: commonest at 1-5 y.

checks.q: Non-ketotic hypoglycaemia with fat oxidation defect suggests?
checks.why: No ketones → hyperinsulinism or fat-oxidation defect (MCAD).

checks.q: Childhood hyperglycaemia is almost always?
checks.why: Hyperglycaemia in children is almost always type 1 diabetes.

I-10.explain: Fetal islets overrespond to maternal glucose and keep pumping after birth; fast falls in glucose shift water into brain cells.
I-10.hook: No insulin bolus in DKA: protect the brain.

checks.q: Infants of diabetic mothers become hypoglycaemic because of?
checks.why: Maternal hyperglycaemia → fetal hyperinsulinism → hypo and macrosomia.

checks.q: Insulin bolus in DKA risks which complication?
checks.why: Rapid osmotic shifts → cerebral oedema.

I-10.explain: Early adrenaline response gives autonomic signs; later the brain runs out of fuel causing neuroglycopenia.

checks.q: Which is a neuroglycopenic sign?
checks.why: Autonomic: sweating, tremor, tachycardia; neuroglycopenic: confusion, seizures, coma.

I-10.explain: The cause is only visible during the hypo, so sample before correcting; ketones discriminate the groups; DKA is a triad.

checks.q: When is the critical sample taken?
checks.why: Take insulin, C-peptide, cortisol, GH, ketones before giving glucose.

checks.q: Best discriminator in hypoglycaemia work-up?
checks.why: Ketones at the time of the low sugar split ketotic vs non-ketotic.

checks.q: DKA bicarbonate threshold?
checks.why: DKA: glucose + ketosis + pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L (notes).

I-10.explain: Correct sugar quickly with dextrose; then treat the cause specifically; in DKA restore volume before slow insulin.

checks.q: Hypoglycaemia bolus dose?
checks.why: 2 ml/kg 10% dextrose, then infusion; glucagon if no access.

checks.q: First-line drug for hyperinsulinism?
checks.why: Diazoxide inhibits insulin release (octreotide is second-line); cornstarch for GSD; avoid fasting in MCAD.

checks.q: DKA insulin infusion rate?
checks.why: Fluids first, then insulin 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h an hour later, no bolus.

I-11.explain: Reactive nodes are small, tender and self-limiting; persistence, size or hardness push toward malignancy.

checks.q: Reactive nodes typically resolve within?
checks.why: Reactive nodes: soft, tender, <2 cm, resolve in 4-6 weeks.

I-11.explain: Localised nodes drain a local infection; generalised nodes mean systemic infection, inflammation or malignancy.

checks.q: Commonest cause of localised bacterial lymphadenitis?
checks.why: S. aureus > S. pyogenes; also Bartonella, atypical mycobacteria, TB.

checks.q: Which causes generalised lymphadenopathy?
checks.why: Generalised: EBV, CMV, toxo, HIV, Kawasaki, JIA, SLE, leukaemia, lymphoma.

I-11.explain: EBV drives T-cell proliferation; pyogenic nodes liquefy; lymphoma is diagnosed by architecture, and mediastinal nodes can compress the airway.

checks.q: In EBV, which node region shows T-cell hyperplasia?
checks.why: EBV: T-cell hyperplasia in the paracortex.

checks.q: Staph/Strep lymphadenitis can progress to?
checks.why: Suppuration → abscess with fluctuance.

checks.q: Why is excisional rather than needle sampling needed for lymphoma?
checks.why: Lymphoma diagnosis depends on architecture; mediastinal mass threatens airway.

I-11.explain: EBV gives a recognisable syndrome; red-flag node features suggest malignancy; atypical mycobacteria give a cold purple node.

checks.q: EBV typically causes which nodes?
checks.why: EBV: fatigue, fever, posterior cervical nodes, pharyngitis, HSM.

checks.q: Which node site is worrying?
checks.why: Worrying: >2 cm and growing, >6 weeks, supraclavicular, painless.

checks.q: Cold, violaceous, non-tender node in a toddler suggests?
checks.why: Atypical mycobacteria: violaceous, painless node in toddlers.

I-11.explain: Blood count and film detect leukaemia quickly; CXR before anaesthesia avoids airway collapse from a mediastinal mass.

checks.q: Highest-yield first test in lymphadenopathy?
checks.why: FBC and film first; CRP, LDH, urate, EBV/CMV serology.

checks.q: What must be done before node biopsy?
checks.why: CXR looks for a mediastinal mass threatening the airway under anaesthesia.

I-11.explain: Most nodes are reactive and only need watching; when lymphoma is suspected take the whole node.

checks.q: Soft, mobile, non-tender nodes are managed by?
checks.why: Observation: reactive nodes resolve in 4-6 weeks.

checks.q: Biopsy type for suspected lymphoma?
checks.why: Excisional biopsy preserves architecture; FNA is inadequate.

I-12.explain: Septic arthritis destroys a joint in hours, so it is excluded before anything else.

checks.q: What must be excluded first in a child with joint pain?
checks.why: Septic arthritis is joint-destroying and must be excluded first.

I-12.explain: Group causes into reactive, inflammatory, malignant, mechanical and septic; age predicts mechanical ones.
I-12.hook: DDH baby, Perthes child, SUFE teen.

checks.q: Rheumatic fever arises through which mechanism?
checks.why: Anti-M protein antibodies cross-react with host tissue.

checks.q: Typical age of Perthes disease?
checks.why: Perthes 4-8 y; DDH infancy; SUFE obese adolescent.

checks.q: Osteomyelitis in sickle cell is classically due to?
checks.why: Septic arthritis: S. aureus; sickle cell osteomyelitis: Salmonella.

I-12.explain: Slow, looping metaphyseal capillaries let bacteria settle, so osteomyelitis begins there.
I-12.hook: Bugs park in the metaphyseal hairpin loops.

checks.q: Where does haematogenous osteomyelitis start?
checks.why: Slow-flowing hairpin capillary loops in the metaphysis.

I-12.explain: Toxicity and fever separate septic from transient synovitis; timing of pain hints at the cause; Jones criteria define rheumatic fever.
I-12.hook: Morning inflammatory, evening mechanical, night malignant.

checks.q: Afebrile, well child with a limp suggests?
checks.why: Septic: febrile, toxic; transient synovitis: afebrile, well.

checks.q: Night-time bone pain suggests which cause?
checks.why: Morning = inflammatory, after activity = mechanical, night = malignant.

checks.q: Which is a major Jones criterion?
checks.why: Major: carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, nodules.

I-12.explain: Kocher criteria estimate septic risk; aspirate to confirm; JIA is defined by age and duration.

checks.q: Kocher criterion temperature threshold?
checks.why: Kocher: non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5, ESR >40, WBC >12.

checks.q: Imaging of choice for osteomyelitis?
checks.why: MRI shows early marrow oedema; X-ray changes lag ~10-14 days.

checks.q: JIA requires arthritis lasting at least?
checks.why: JIA: onset before 16, lasting ≥ 6 weeks.

I-12.explain: Get the organism before antibiotics, then wash out; NSAIDs for benign or inflammatory disease; prevent rheumatic recurrence with penicillin.

checks.q: In septic arthritis, when is the joint aspirated?
checks.why: Aspirate first for culture, then IV antibiotics + washout.

checks.q: First-line DMARD in JIA?
checks.why: JIA: weekly methotrexate; transient synovitis: rest and NSAIDs.

checks.q: Rheumatic fever prophylaxis if penicillin anaphylaxis?
checks.why: Penicillin prophylaxis; macrolides if anaphylaxis.

I-13.explain: DRE confirms blood and finds fissures/masses; haemodynamics decide urgency; then age and story narrow the cause.

checks.q: First test in a child with bloody stool?
checks.why: DRE and haemodynamics first (university exam answer).

I-13.explain: Each age has its own bleeders: neonates swallowed blood or NEC, toddlers fissures, older children colitis.

checks.q: Which neonatal cause of 'bloody stool' isn't the baby's blood?
checks.why: Swallowed maternal blood is common; confirm with Apt test.

checks.q: Commonest cause of bloody stool in toddlers?
checks.why: Fissure is commonest; also intussusception, Meckel's, polyp.

checks.q: Which causes bloody stool in older children?
checks.why: Older: infectious colitis, IBD, HSP, HUS.

I-13.explain: Ectopic gastric acid ulcerates neighbouring ileum; Meckel's follows the rule of 2s; shiga toxin injures endothelium, and antibiotics release more.

checks.q: Why does a Meckel's diverticulum bleed?
checks.why: Acid from ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates adjacent ileum.

checks.q: Rule of 2s: Meckel's lies how far from the ileocaecal valve?
checks.why: 2% of people, 2 feet from valve, 2 inches long, under age 2.

checks.q: Antibiotics in E. coli O157 infection do what?
checks.why: Antibiotics increase shiga toxin release → HUS risk.

I-13.explain: Pain pattern and vomiting separate surgical causes: colicky pain → intussusception, painless big bleed → Meckel's, bilious vomit → volvulus.
I-13.hook: Bilious vomit = volvulus until proven otherwise.

checks.q: Paroxysmal pain with sausage-shaped mass suggests?
checks.why: Intussusception (3 mo-3 y): paroxysmal pain + sausage mass.

checks.q: Painless, transfusion-requiring rectal bleeding suggests?
checks.why: Painless massive bleeding without diarrhoea = Meckel's (exam answer).

checks.q: Bilious vomiting plus blood suggests?
checks.why: Bilious vomiting + blood = volvulus, a surgical emergency.

I-13.explain: Apt distinguishes fetal from maternal haemoglobin; a technetium scan shows gastric mucosa; ultrasound shows the target; HUS is a triad.

checks.q: Which test detects swallowed maternal blood?
checks.why: Apt test distinguishes maternal (adult) from fetal Hb.

checks.q: Imaging for suspected Meckel's?
checks.why: Tc-99m pertechnetate is taken up by gastric mucosa; intussusception → US target sign.

checks.q: Which is part of the HUS triad?
checks.why: HUS: haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, AKI.

I-13.explain: Resuscitate first; then cause-specific: air/contrast enema for intussusception, surgery for volvulus, bowel rest for NEC, no antibiotics in HUS.

checks.q: A shocked child with bloody stool needs first?
checks.why: Resuscitate first: wide-bore access, fluids, cross-match.

checks.q: First-line treatment of intussusception?
checks.why: Enema reduction; volvulus → theatre; NEC → stop feeds, decompress, antibiotics.

checks.q: Antibiotics in HUS from E. coli O157?
checks.why: No antibiotics: they increase toxin release.

I-14.explain: Swallowed blood from the nose or mother's nipple, or red food, mimics haematemesis; confirm source first.
I-14.hook: Is it theirs, and is it gut?

checks.q: First step in apparent haematemesis?
options: Confirm it's the child's GI blood
checks.why: Confirm the blood is the child's own and from the GI tract.

I-14.explain: Split non-variceal (mucosal) from variceal (portal hypertension); neonates swallow maternal blood or lack vitamin K.

checks.q: Which is a non-variceal upper GI bleed cause?
checks.why: Non-variceal: oesophagitis, gastritis, PUD, Mallory-Weiss, button battery.

checks.q: Which neonatal procedure predisposes to varices?
checks.why: UVC → portal vein thrombosis → portal hypertension.

checks.q: Which neonatal bleeding cause is preventable?
checks.why: Neonate: swallowed maternal blood, vitamin K deficiency bleeding (prevented by prophylaxis).

I-14.explain: Pre-hepatic block raises portal pressure with a normal liver; batteries generate current and alkali that burn through tissue fast.

checks.q: Portal vein thrombosis causes which type of portal hypertension?
checks.why: Portal vein thrombosis = pre-hepatic portal hypertension → varices.

checks.q: A swallowed button battery can erode into?
checks.why: Necrosis within hours can erode into the aorta (aorto-oesophageal fistula).

I-14.explain: Portal hypertension signs suggest varices; multi-site neonatal bleeding suggests a coagulation factor deficiency.

checks.q: Splenomegaly with haematemesis suggests?
checks.why: Splenomegaly, ascites, caput medusae, low platelets → variceal.

checks.q: Neonate bleeding from several sites suggests?
checks.why: Multi-site bleeding in a neonate = vitamin K deficiency.

I-14.explain: Exclude mimics first, then decide variceal vs non-variceal because the drugs and endoscopic approach differ.

checks.q: Which is a haematemesis impostor?
checks.why: Exclude epistaxis, cracked nipple (Apt test), red foods.

checks.q: Why split variceal from non-variceal?
checks.why: Variceal vs non-variceal determines treatment.

I-14.explain: Resuscitate and correct clotting; vasoactive drugs + antibiotics + banding for varices; PPI + endoscopy for mucosal bleeds; batteries out now.

checks.q: Coagulopathy in GI bleeding is corrected with?
checks.why: Two large cannulas, cross-match; vitamin K + FFP for coagulopathy.

checks.q: Vasoactive drug for variceal bleeding?
checks.why: Terlipressin or octreotide + prophylactic antibiotics + band ligation.

checks.q: Non-variceal bleed: drug given with endoscopy?
checks.why: High-dose PPI + endoscopy; button battery → emergency removal.

I-15.explain: Most proteinuria is trivial; confirm it's real and quantify it. Pyuria is treated as infection until culture says otherwise.

checks.q: Leukocyturia is regarded as what until culture negative?
checks.why: Leukocyturia = UTI until culture negative.

I-15.explain: Benign transient/orthostatic proteinuria dominates; nephrotic children 1-10 y almost always have minimal change; sterile pyuria has a short list.

checks.q: Commonest cause of proteinuria in children?
checks.why: Commonest: transient; orthostatic in upright overweight adolescents.

checks.q: Nephrotic syndrome age 1-10 is usually due to?
checks.why: Minimal change ~90% at age 1-10.

checks.q: Which causes sterile pyuria?
checks.why: Sterile pyuria: partially treated UTI, renal TB, Kawasaki, appendicitis.

I-15.explain: Protein loss drops albumin, causing oedema and liver lipid overproduction; PSGN consumes C3 via the alternative pathway and resolves.

checks.q: Nephrotic syndrome albumin threshold?
checks.why: Nephrotic: heavy proteinuria, oedema, albumin <30 g/L (notes), hyperlipidaemia.

checks.q: PSGN after pharyngitis follows by how long?
checks.why: Throat 1-2 weeks, skin 3-6 weeks; low C3, normal C4, normal by 8 weeks.

I-15.explain: Nephrotic losses of antibodies and anticoagulant proteins cause infection and clots; nephritic is inflammation with blood, casts and hypertension.
I-15.hook: Nephrotic: protein out; nephritic: blood out.

checks.q: Which is a nephrotic complication?
checks.why: SBP, renal vein thrombosis, PE (loss of antithrombin, immunoglobulin).

checks.q: Red cell casts indicate?
checks.why: Nephritic: haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, milder proteinuria.

I-15.explain: Dipstick screens, first-morning sample rules out orthostatic, ratio quantifies; nitrites are specific, LE sensitive; image after UTI to find reflux/scars.
I-15.hook: DMSA for scars, MCUG for reflux.

checks.q: How is proteinuria quantified?
checks.why: Urinalysis → first-morning urine → protein:creatinine ratio.

checks.q: Which urine dipstick marker is specific for UTI?
checks.why: Nitrites specific, leucocyte esterase sensitive.

checks.q: Which scan detects renal scarring after UTI?
checks.why: Ultrasound → MCUG (reflux) → DMSA (scarring).

I-15.explain: Typical nephrotic children respond to steroids so biopsy is skipped; nephritic disease can progress, needing specialist input.

checks.q: Typical nephrotic syndrome aged 1-10 is treated with?
checks.why: Typical 1-10 y nephrotic → steroids without biopsy.

checks.q: Nephritic syndrome requires?
checks.why: Nephritic → urgent nephrology.
